title: NHS faces more challenging winter than normal, health secretary warns
description: The NHS is facing a more challenging winter than normal, the health secretary has said, after multiple heatwaves led to its busiest summer on record i
body: The NHS is facing a more challenging winter than normal, the health secretary has said, after multiple heatwaves led to its busiest summer on record in England.Yvette Cooper announced £140m funding to boost urgent care capacity as part of an effort to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses, including flu and norovirus.The money will go towards 14 schemes across England, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.Shadow health secretary Damian Hinds said the government needed to act, but asked it to explain where the money was coming from. The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) England said the funding was "just another sticking plaster".Cooper said: "Winter will be more challenging for our NHS this year, after such a heavy summer."That's why we have been preparing early and investing in extra urgent care capacity to help get patients the care they need."It comes after almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August in England, according to NHS data, the highest ever figure for a summer period.Health thinktank the King's Fund warned that the service was facing a "twin crisis" going into the winter, with little time between peak periods for staff and the system to recover.NHS leaders are urging eligible people to get flu vaccinations, with medical director Prof Frankie Swords saying there were "ominous" signs of winter pressure already affecting hospitals.Swords said earlier this month there were more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year. "And unfortunately, people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she added. NHS executive director Emma Rowland said this winter would be tough for the health service, but the investment in urgent care would help more patients get "the right care on the right place, at the right time".RCN England's executive director Patricia Marquis said the extra money was welcome in the short term but would ultimately provide "just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point"."The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff," she said.The waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row, according to the latest data.An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.These were the highest numbers since October 2025, and have raised questions as to whether the NHS will meet the government's target to treat 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.

schema.headline: NHS faces more challenging winter than normal, health secretary warns

title: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,200 arrested
description: Figure caption, How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across FranceByJack BurgessUpdated 2 hours agoViolence broke out across France on
body: Figure caption, How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across FranceByJack BurgessUpdated 2 hours agoViolence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living.At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest.In the French capital, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC that they were "pacifists" who were "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".Figure caption, Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protestsHowever, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fireA young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15- to 18-year-olds.Their numbers have been bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups. These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes (or "yellow vest") movement, which demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for more than a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.Image source, ReutersImage caption, A car was set alight at the Place de la République in ParisWhile France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.Image source, ReutersImage caption, French riot police walk past a burning barricade amid clashes with protesters on 17 October Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers during a television interview on 8 October.However, the protests have continued and intensified.

schema.headline: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,200 arrested

title: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence
description: Figure caption, John Swinney said son is 'reason' for independenceByScotland political editorThis was a more emotional speech than we are used to from
body: Figure caption, John Swinney said son is 'reason' for independenceByScotland political editorThis was a more emotional speech than we are used to from John Swinney. His voice quivered as he explained that his personal commitment to the cause is for the future of his 15-year-old son, Matthew.Then the autocue stalled and the SNP leader is heard saying under his breath "oh, come on".A period of silence was broken by the conference crowd who came to his rescue with a standing ovation.Without the prime minister's name being mentioned, this section of the speech seemed to be a response to Andy Burnham's emotional appeal for the union in memory of his father at the Labour conference in Liverpool.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Andy Burnham has called for greater devolution in Scotland earlier this weekThere was a more obvious dig at the prime minister, who visited Motherwell this week to promote regional devolution within Scotland and drew on his experience as mayor of Greater Manchester.Again, without mentioning Andy Burnham by name, the first minister said: "Some think we should just be like Manchester. Well, I'm afraid I disagree."Scotland is no city. We are no region. We are a nation and soon we will be an independent nation."That went down well in the conference hall - even if the first minister is perfectly prepared to work with the prime minister on plans to create a regional level of government in Scotland, with powers transferred from both Westminster and Holyrood.Swinney also claimed that independence is "very close" in the full knowledge that there will not be another referendum unless there is a sustained surge in public support for Scottish statehood.Pledges on buses and misogynyPart of his strategy for achieving that is to demonstrate delivery in devolved government on issues of everyday concern.That's why he highlighted the roll out of the Scottish government's £2 bus fare cap as an example of cost of living support.It is already in place in the Highlands and across west central Scotland, and now he has confirmed its extension across north east Scotland from April.It should be available everywhere in Scotland by the end of this parliamentary term, by which time he said the Scottish government would, through franchising and regulation, have taken the bus network under public control.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, John Swinney, pictured with his son Matthew and wife, Elizabeth Quigley, at the SNP conference Announcements on making misogyny a specific criminal offence and new funding for community groups to fight racism are also designed to demonstrate a sense of immediate purpose.His speech seemed to energise those in the hall who are already with him. He also hopes it will engage those across Scotland who might be open to considering independence.Earlier this week, Swinney told me he is loving being first minister and intends to lead the SNP into the next Scottish Parliament election in 2031.However long he stays in office, this will always be a special conference for him - his first since leading his party through a successful Holyrood campaign and the one where he put the personal into his political commitment to independence.

schema.headline: Swinney's emotional explanation for his commitment to independence

title: Man City 3-2 Ipswich: Boos and bananas on day of defiance at Etihad Stadium
description: Figure caption, Haaland nets double as Man City go six points clear at the topByNeil JohnstonBBC Sport football reporterIt started with Manchester Cit
body: Figure caption, Haaland nets double as Man City go six points clear at the topByNeil JohnstonBBC Sport football reporterIt started with Manchester City supporters booing the Premier League anthem and ended with Phil Foden taking an inflatable banana into his Match of the Day interview after helping see off Ipswich to pull six points clear at the top of the table.On a day of defiance in east Manchester, City's fans made their feelings crystal clear in their first top-flight home game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.Tens of thousands inside Etihad Stadium booed and jeered when the Premier League anthem was played over the speakers shortly before kick-off, then they started chanting 'City, City, City'.The anger did not last.There was a chant about playing Stockport away and the gallows humour continued when City fans sang 'You're going down with the City' to Ipswich's travelling support.City boss Enzo Maresca, who is the first manager in Premier League history to win his first seven games in charge, said afterwards he felt the air of defiance from the stands even before kick-off."The environment was very good," said the Italian after a game watched by 60,817, a new record crowd at Etihad Stadium."The fans, the club and the players are all together on this journey."Figure caption, Manchester City manager Maresca reacts to win against Ipswich TownCity fans go bananasCity fans arrived at the ground to find hundreds of inflatable bananas had been placed on seats in the home sections for fans to wave throughout the game.They were visible in the away end at Liverpool last week but this was on a different scale and the Etihad was turned into a sea of yellow.The inflatables are a flashback to the late '80s when what began as a light-hearted joke soon turned into one of the most memorable fan crazes in English football.They are enjoying a revival at a time when City have appealed after being found guilty of charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, and creating 'sham contracts' to inflate sponsorship deals by £830m.There were surreal scenes at one point on Saturday as fans jeered during the Premier League anthem while waving the inflatables in the air."You can tell they are behind us and they're pushing us," Phil Foden said when asked about the fans after scoring on his return to the side following suspension after being sent off against Manchester United on 13 September.Foden's 19th-minute opener was his first goal of 2026."It's nice to play at home and you can hear how loud they are," he added. "They're giving us that extra boost that we need."Figure caption, Man City's players and fans 'fueled' by boos and bananas'I didn't expect to win seven out of seven'Taking over from Pep Guardiola - 20 trophies during 10 seasons in charge - was always going to be a big challenge for Maresca.Seven matches in, City's Premier League record remains flawless.No points dropped, seven wins out of seven despite falling behind against Bournemouth and playing for more than an hour with 10 men at Manchester United."For sure I didn't expect to win seven out of seven," said Maresca. "We are working well and working good. "I'm very happy especially with the situation in general."Today we controlled the game for 95 minutes. We created chances, we scored. "We finished with a little bit of suffering together but overall, it is good."On Foden's impressive return to action, Maresca added: "I said since day one that I love Phil. I know him from years ago and I know how good he is. "It's a matter of helping him to again be one of the best players in the Premier League."Figure caption, Phil Foden goes bananas!'I give my players credit'Despite the off-field turmoil, this is City's best start to a league season in 129 years.Only Chelsea in 2005-06 (first nine) and Liverpool in 2019-20 (first eight) have ever won the first seven matches of a Premier League campaign.Both went on to win the title."First of all, I am very happy because it's a matter of winning games in this business," said Maresca after the game."We were able to win seven in a row and what made me very happy was day by day with the players, the way they are working and how I can see them improving."Today I thought we controlled the game, created chances and [were] good off the ball. We are doing well and I think that's the most important thing."On his players dealing with the events surrounding the club off the field, Maresca said: "They are not worried about people who judge from outside because they know people are trying to judge them."Inside, I promise the players are happy. They're getting credit and I give credit to them."Follow Manchester City on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical City contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about City

schema.headline: Man City 3-2 Ipswich: Boos and bananas on day of defiance at Etihad Stadium

title: Three takeaways from Elon Musk's latest political donations
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByAna FaguyWashington DCBillionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk is once again pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into a US elec
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByAna FaguyWashington DCBillionaire Tesla CEO Elon Musk is once again pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into a US election - this time with the aim of helping Republicans maintain their control of Congress.Musk donated upwards of $200m (£150m) in the quarter that ended on 30 September, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings reviewed by the BBC.The fillings were released just over two weeks before the 2026 midterm election, in which many races are close and Republicans risk losing their majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate. Musk also put significant money - $290m - and effort into helping elect US President Donald Trump and other Republicans in 2024.Here is where the richest person in the world has been donating this time around and what it might mean for his businesses. Most of the donations went to one groupThe bulk of the money donated last quarter by the world's only trillionaire, $158m, went to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) Pac, the filings showed.It is one of the largest publicly known single political donations in US history and some have suggested it is the biggest ever.SLF is a super Pac - which stands for Political Action Committee - backing Republican Senate candidates in tough races. Super Pacs are independent committees that can raise unlimited amounts of money and play a major role in funding US political campaigns.It quickly sent the money on to a group supporting Texas Republican Ken Paxton. The state attorney general is at risk of losing to Democrat James Talarico in a race for a seat his party has held for decades. They have been polling neck and neck and the election's outcome is considered a bellwether for the future of Republican power.Musk also donated more than $80m to the America Pac that he founded during the 2024 election.Texas is a key focus for MuskAmerica Pac spent millions on digital communications, postal campaigning and phone calls opposing Talarico last quarter, as well as thousands on political marketing to support Paxton.At the same time, Musk donated another $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, a group primarily backing Paxton, records show.The flow of money highlights a major theme for Musk: Texas.In recent years, the tech CEO has been moving his business empire -  including SpaceX, Tesla and X - to the southern US state after expressing frustration with operating in California.Texas has offered Musk fewer government regulations and no state personal income tax and no corporate income tax.Keeping politicians who favour looser government restrictions in charge, as Republicans typically have, could help maintain that environment for Musk.And his big spending in Texas and in the Texas Senate race seems to point to Musk's understanding of that, political analyst Cayce Myers told the BBC."Republicans have a fundraising advantage this time, but fundraising by itself does not actually guarantee success," he said.A broader trend for tech executivesFor many voters this year, technology has become a top issue. People across the country are pushing for increased government oversight of artificial intelligence,  data centres and social media.That's something that has tech leaders like Musk developing closer ties to the Republican party, which historically has promoted lighter government regulation, Myers said."What [tech leaders] are looking at is a future where there is growing demand and call for regulation and I think they want to be in an advantageous position," he said. "We're seeing them shift, and fall behind Republicans."Other tech leaders, such as OpenAI president and his wife Greg and Anna Brockman are also putting big money behind Republicans.The couple donated $25m to the Trump-aligned Maga Inc Pac last year.Myer noted it's not just the tech sector but industries like cryptocurrency and gambling where large sums of money are being donated in an attempt to exert influence."This is the idea of shaping the regulatory environment through contributions," he said.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Three takeaways from Elon Musk's latest political donations

title: Student who spells by blinking is denied chance to sit exam
description: Tracey Campbell, of Rett UK, said Romi had been dismissed in many areas of her life and she wanted to prove she was capable."To have these extra barri
body: Tracey Campbell, of Rett UK, said Romi had been dismissed in many areas of her life and she wanted to prove she was capable."To have these extra barriers put in place is completely unfair and unjust," she said."What has been fabulous about exam boards in England is that people have been allowed to sit their exams over a long period of time, one question at a time."Glasgow Clyde College, where Romi studies, said she is "highly capable and committed".Claire Donaghey, assistant principal arts and continuing education, said: "Despite considerable discussion with Qualifications Scotland, the mitigating arrangements we have proposed have not been deemed compatible with these requirements."We remain fully committed to supporting Romi and will continue to work constructively with her, her family and Qualifications Scotland to explore every available option and achieve the best possible outcome for her."Qualifications Scotland said it was committed to making reasonable adjustments so that disabled learners have an equal opportunity to demonstrate their knowledge, skills and understanding. A spokesperson said: "This year over 39,000 learners benefited from assessment arrangements. "We also have a duty to maintain the integrity of qualifications, so must always ensure that any reasonable adjustments put in place for learners do not impact standards."

schema.headline: Student who spells by blinking is denied chance to sit exam

title: Florian Wirtz delivers for Liverpool - but is playmaker Andoni Iraola's great conundrum?
description: Figure caption, Liverpool come from behind to beat nine-man BrentfordByHarry PooleBBC Sport journalistFlorian Wirtz was instrumental as Liverpool retu
body: Figure caption, Liverpool come from behind to beat nine-man BrentfordByHarry PooleBBC Sport journalistFlorian Wirtz was instrumental as Liverpool returned to winning ways in the Premier League at Brentford on Saturday, but does the German playmaker remain boss Andoni Iraola's greatest conundrum?Wirtz has come in for criticism amid his struggles to replicate the form which persuaded the Reds to pay Bayer Leverkusen what was a club record £116m in June 2025.Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard even said this week that the 23-year-old could benefit from being taken out of the team altogether, to overcome what the club's former captain perceives as a lack of confidence.The key dilemma facing Iraola was again evident in west London on Saturday.Liverpool bounced back from their first league defeat of the season against Manchester City last weekend by scoring twice in the second half against a Brentford side reduced to 10 men before half-time.The visitors produced plenty of chances, particularly with their man advantage in the second half when they registered 14 of their total 21 attempts.Wirtz was at the heart of things in the final third.The Germany international created more chances from open play (nine) than any other player has managed in a Premier League game over the past six seasons.The last player to create as many chances in a single game in the competition was Sadio Mane, for Liverpool against Burnley, in January 2021 (also nine).In an away game, he is the first player to reach that tally in more than 15 years, since Samir Nasri registered 10 for Manchester City against Tottenham in August 2011.Image caption, Florian Wirtz completed 53 of the 65 passes he attempted (81.5%) - including a match-leading 38 inside the final thirdDespite answering his critics with those standout statistics, the impact of his playing style on the dynamic of the team continues to come under scrutiny.BBC Sport pundit and former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy believes a midfield which features Wirtz as the number 10 remains a problem as it makes Iraola's side too easy to play against."They got the job done. First and foremost, that's another win on the road, which is always positive," Murphy said of Liverpool's performance."But I thought they looked too easy to play against. The spaces are too big. "They're playing with two wingers and Wirtz at 10, so they're relying heavily on the two midfield players to try and cover so much space. "It was too easy for Brentford to play out and to get in behind. That would be the biggest concern today for me."Wirtz's strengths are clear.Following his latest performance, no player has created more chances in the Premier League this season. He is level with Brighton's Pascal Gross on 18.He played in Munoz to begin Liverpool's fightback, meaning Wirtz has assisted in back-to-back games for Liverpool across all competitions for the first time - although this was only his second goal involvement in seven league games this term.He was at the heart of Liverpool's attack, with a match-leading 12 final-third entries and 37 passes in the final third.However, only Milos Kerkez (20) lost possession on more occasions than Wirtz (19) among Liverpool players, and he won just one of his nine duels."They don't look solid and don't look together in terms of shape," Murphy said."Instead of a number 10, where Wirtz is struggling to impact games, put three midfielders in."Always, the priority is foundation, defence, stability, being hard to beat. The other stuff can follow from there. "At the moment, it just looks a little bit open. Against better teams, you're going to get hurt."Figure caption, Liverpool players in 'delicate' situation over 'demanding' schedule - IraolaVictory took Liverpool up to fifth in the table, with three wins from their first seven league games under Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot in the summer.The Spaniard oversaw the Reds' first away league win after conceding first since December 2023, ending a run of 19 winless away games when going 1-0 behind.But, while striker Alexander Isak returned from injury, Iraola was dealt fresh blows as Dominik Szoboszlai and Jeremie Frimpong suffered injuries on Saturday.Iraola told BBC Sport: "When you come here, you see the results of Brentford at home and you have to be ready for this kind of battle. "We had a lot of chances. Even at the end, we had some counters where we were three against one and need to finish. When we go 2-1, every throw-in and every free-kick can be a problem."We are in a delicate situation with some of the players. We were talking about this run of four games in 10 days, it's very, very demanding. "We have to rest again because we have another big, big game against Villarreal [in the Champions League on Tuesday]."Figure caption, Liverpool fan delighted with Florian Wirtz's performance at BrentfordFollow Liverpool on BBC SoundsPre-match, post-match and topical Reds contentSubscribe and listen for everything you love about Liverpool

schema.headline: Florian Wirtz delivers for Liverpool - but is playmaker Andoni Iraola's great conundrum?

title: Dubois vs Wardley 2: Londoner retains title with dominant second-round stoppage
description: Daniel Dubois underlined his status as Britain's leading heavyweight with a devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain his WBO title
body: Daniel Dubois underlined his status as Britain's leading heavyweight with a devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain his WBO title in London.The 29-year-old floored Wardley with a straight right inside the opening 20 seconds of their eagerly anticipated rematch at the O2 Arena and continued his relentless assault.Wardley survived the opening round but was overwhelmed by another sustained attack in the second, prompting his corner to throw in the towel.Dubois registers a second successive stoppage victory over Wardley, just five months after climbing off the canvas twice to dethrone his British rival in a thrilling 11-round contest in Manchester.This time, there was no such drama for the champion, who was dominant from the opening bell as he extended his professional record to 24 wins - 23 by knockout - and three defeats."Fabio is a great boy, coming in for the second time, but it was my time and my era. I had my intentions, bad intentions from the beginning," Dubois said. "My back was against the wall the first time, this time we just had to go out there and show that we mean business, which is what we did tonight."Wardley, 31, suffered the second defeat of his 23-fight professional career."I have always thrown myself in with the best competitors out there, the best in the business, the biggest, hardest, meanest guys around so, there is no shame in a loss when you're testing yourself against the best," he said.A sell-out crowd of 19,000 packed the O2 Arena and made their allegiances clear.Wardley's charismatic yet measured personality has made him a popular figure. He looked full of purpose as he took his time on stage, fireworks exploding in front of him, his usual smile replaced by a look of determination.Dubois, meanwhile, was greeted by jeers as he marched straight past the fireworks and towards the ring, wasting little time soaking up the occasion. Actor Paddy Considine, comedian Rob Beckett, Oasis star Noel Gallagher and darts world champion Luke Littler were among the famous faces in attendance.With 41 knockouts between the fighters, few expected the judges to be called upon. The feeling beforehand was that Wardley's best chance lay in making another fast start, having dropped Dubois inside the opening moments of their first meeting.But in a stunning reversal, it took just 17 seconds for Wardley to hit the canvas as Dubois backed him into a corner and landed a straight right.Chants of 'oh Fabio Wardley' were quickly silenced as Dubois continued to unload punishing combinations. Another furious attack towards the end of the round left Wardley in deep trouble.Trainer Ben Davison, criticised for not withdrawing Wardley sooner in their first contest, stood poised with a towel in his hand as his fighter survived to the bell. There had already been concerns over whether Wardley had returned too quickly after the punishment he absorbed in May, when he was left bloodied and badly swollen.And those fears appeared justified as the challenger struggled to cope with Dubois' relentless pressure. Wardley's hands were low and his punches wild and telegraphed, lacking the menace he had shown in Manchester.Backed into the corner again in the second round, he was subjected to another barrage before Davison leapt up and threw in the towel.Dubois continues to fly the flag for British heavyweight boxing. After losing to Oleksandr Usyk in 2023, he responded with impressive victories over Jarrell Miller, Filip Hrgovic and Anthony Joshua, only to suffer another defeat by Usyk last year.But back-to-back stoppage victories over Wardley have reinforced his standing among the world's leading active heavyweights.IBF champion Hrgovic, whom Dubois stopped in June 2024, entered the ring afterwards, with both men keen on a rematch.However, promoter Frank Warren wants Hrgovic to make his first title defence in Croatia before pursuing a unification fight.The biggest payday for Dubois could come against the winner of Joshua and Tyson Fury's December showdown, which is expected to have the WBA 'super' title at stake.Asked who he wants to face next, Dubois said: "Whoever is next in line, really. I'm the champion now, and I want to get some big fights in. At this stage in my career, big money, big fights."For Wardley, successive defeats represent a significant setback, but his remarkable journey should not be forgotten.The former recruitment consultant had just four white-collar fights before turning professional in 2017. Less than a decade later, he was a world heavyweight champion.Rather than rebuild against lesser opposition following May's punishing defeat, Wardley gambled on an immediate rematch with one of the division's most destructive punchers.It was a gamble that backfired and, after two bruising defeats, he may benefit from some time away.

schema.headline: Dubois vs Wardley 2: Londoner retains title with dominant second-round stoppage

title: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions
description: Figure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic correspondentSuspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman.
body: Figure caption, Watch: How does music on The Traitors manipulate your emotions?ByMusic correspondentSuspicion, intrigue, treachery, Claudia Winkleman. The Traitors has it all.But the shadowiest of the show's shadowy secrets is its music.Have you ever noticed how the soundtrack manipulates your perception? A sinister orchestral flourish hints at a double cross. A cheeky chord injects humour into a kitchen conflab.As ever, though, you shouldn't trust what happens in the castle. The music can provide emphasis or act as misdirection, all at the producers' behest.Duplicity was baked into the music from the beginning."I remember the BBC was quite reluctant to even think about a show with murder as a main feature, so I knew I didn't want the music to go really dark," says Sam Watts, who composed the opening theme and much of the incidental score (but is not responsible for the show's haunting cover versions of well-known pop songs... more on those later).Watts, who had previously worked on Planet Earth and The Sarah Jane Adventures, pitched to work on the programme with only a basic idea of the set-up. It was only when he learned Winkleman was the host that he settled on his approach."They sent me a little shot they'd done of the opening with Claudia and the castle. That's when I knew it was going to be a bit camp and high drama and all the glorious things that Claudia brings to the show. So I just went with that - dark but fun."Image source, Sam WattsImage caption, Sam Watts' Traitors theme helped to establish the show's identityFor the title sequence, the 44-year-old wanted something memorable. As a kid, his favourite song was Bernard Hoffer's gloriously over-the-top Thundercats theme, external, so that's the level he aspired to."I was trying to write something that signified the show was starting, so that people would run in from making their cup of tea in the kitchen to watch it."And I wanted a memorable melody that people could hum, because it helps with the identity of the show."The Traitors theme is "one of the biggest pieces of music I've ever written", he says, recorded with a full orchestra and overdubbed with dozens of electronic elements to create a heightened, hyperreal atmosphere.That bled into the 20 or so other pieces Watts wrote, which also appear in dozens of international spin-offs.The idea, he says, is that the whole hour feels like a film trailer, with viewers permanently waiting for the psychological pressure chamber to explode.To achieve that, he employed several techniques of trailer music - most notably the "Braam", a klaxon-like punctuation mark invented for Christopher Nolan's Inception (see video for a fuller exploration).Show producer Sarah Fay took that concept and amplified it. "We wanted to just supersize it and make it feel like a drama, not like your usual reality [show]," she said in a rare interview with Metro, external when the first civilian series aired in 2022."We wanted to make it feel like that edge-of-your-seat cinematic drama with, you know, elements of Succession, and we wanted it to feel like Knives Out when you get into the castle!"To achieve that, she commissioned additional music from film trailer composers, including Hans Zimmer's company Bleeding Fingers. But she also sprinkled in a handful of creepy cover versions.Some became instant classics - such as a sinister spin on Britney Spears' Toxic, external, or a version of Tears For Fears' Mad World, external seemingly broadcast on a tannoy from Hades.They're so integral to The Traitors' aesthetic that it might surprise you to learn they weren't recorded specifically for the show.Image caption, The Traitors score has proved so popular that an entire BBC Proms concert was devoted to the show's music last yearBoth examples were created by German writer-producers 2wei.Based in Hamburg, they had no idea their music had appeared in The Traitors until friends in the UK messaged them in excitement."We were just flipping out," says 2wei's Simon Heeger. "It's completely different to how we ever thought it would be used."Heeger founded 2wei, pronounced "zwei", in 2016 with his old college friend Christian Vorländer.They had both spent time in LA working on advertisements and (stop me if you're sensing a theme here) film trailers, before moving home to build a music production empire."Christian worked on the Mad Max soundtrack, which is really known for the big drums and the orchestral scale – and that was really the starting point of our sound," says Heeger."Whenever you hear big epic drums with an orchestral sound and maybe a female vocal on top of it, it's usually something we had our fingers in."Image source, 2weiImage caption, Simon Heeger is the co-founder of 2wei, which is responsible for some of Traitors' most memorable cover songsTheir big break came with a stormy reworking of Destiny's Child's Survivor, which featured in the trailer to Alicia Vikander's Tomb Raider, external.Since then, their music has appeared in films like Wonder Woman and video games such as League of Legends. In The Traitors, original 2wei songs like Blindside, external now feature alongside their covers (other producers, including SYML and Damned Anthem also contribute songs to the show).Heeger says their background in commercials makes the music perfectly suited to the show's slippery skullduggery."In adverts, you only have a few seconds to convey a certain emotion and, especially in Traitors, where there are cliffhangers and moments that you don't expect, you need music that comes to the point right away but still has a boldness to it."It's a sweet spot, and it's not easy to convey, but every now and then it works quite well."Fans agree. On Spotify, there are hundreds of playlists dedicated to the programme's background music. Some are tailored to murder mystery parties and Halloween events. Others compile more sedate moments under labels like "gentle tension" or "chill elder emo watching Traitors".But never forget: the soundtrack is playing a deceitful game of its own."A lot of my music has a wink in it and, for The Traitors, it's a little silly and slightly over the top," says Watts."I think it helps the nastier side of things - the murder, the plotting - feel a bit more fun."

schema.headline: How The Traitors' music plays with your emotions

title: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley arena in one turbulent year
description: A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the follo
body: A few weeks after their appearance on the boat, I meet the group again at Wembley Arena, where they are preparing for their first UK concert the following night.As the staging - complete with giant LED screens and the group's logo - is set up around them, the six members rehearse synchronised choreography alongside their back-up dancers.The group consists of main vocalist Sueda Uluca, lead vocalist Lidya Pınar, sub-vocalist Mina Solak, sub-vocalist and main rapper Zeynep Sude Oktay, lead dancer Hilal Yelekçi and main dancer Esin Bahat.But Wembley is just the beginning of their ambitions."After Wembley, we'll manifest Coachella and other big stages," says Hilal Yelekçi, playing on the group's name.manifest were formed in February last year through the Turkish reality TV talent competition Big5 Türkiye, which saw contestants compete over several months for a place in the group.They were mentored by established Turkish pop stars, including Gülçin Ergül, a former member of girl group Hepsi, who was also a judge on the show.The band's rise has been rapid, and they now have more than six million monthly listeners on Spotify.While in London, they released their first English-language single, TRALALA, which topped YouTube's daily music video chart on its release, ahead of videos from Shakira and Taylor Swift.The music video was also their first to be filmed outside Turkey, with the group working with a largely British production crew in east London."Getting out from that safe zone was a bit stressful for us," says Pınar.Despite their hopes to perform on British and American stages, they're keen to retain their Turkish identity."We want to reach a global audience with our Turkish songs actually, not with English ones," says Sude Oktay."We want to teach people to sing in Turkish."Alongside Turkish girl group Hepsi, manifest cite the Spice Girls among their musical inspirations.Pınar says her favourite Spice Girl is Baby Spice."Because of the pink. I'm pink and blonde, so it's obvious," she laughs.They have also had the chance to meet one of the world's biggest pop stars, Dua Lipa. The British-Albanian singer met manifest backstage before watching them perform at her Sunny Hill Festival in Kosovo in July this year."She came to our backstage and said a lot of great things," one member recalls."We really love her, her songs, her stage presence."On the day of the concert, there was a sense of excitement outside Wembley Arena as fans wearing manifest-branded headbands and carrying banners gathered.The crowd was predominantly Turkish women in their 20s and 30s, many dressed in colours associated with the group. Among them were friends Elif, 31, and Zeynep, 25, both Turkish women living in London, who reflected on the band's past year."I don't think I've ever heard of a girl band performing there," says Zeynep."I think I was seven when Hepsi were last together. It's maybe a once-in-a-lifetime experience."Turkish pop star Tarkan previously performed at Wembley Arena in 2008.For Elif, the concert has a wider significance."We are going through difficult times back home. It means girl power and empowerment, and just having fun and being together," she says."I feel like back home people came together to support them and criticise the treatment that they were receiving from the government."Zeynep adds: "It's great to see them here, but I hope one day they will be back in Turkey and they'll be able to do whatever they want without getting persecuted for it."

schema.headline: Manifest: From reality TV to Wembley arena in one turbulent year

title: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire
description: Figure caption, Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?ByDaniel Thomas and Oliver SmithBusiness reportersWoul
body: Figure caption, Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired?ByDaniel Thomas and Oliver SmithBusiness reportersWould you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job?We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates, external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason. But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating?Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager. He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI."Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that."Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicantsWhile Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on.He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates."That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening."'More competition for students'This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI "at some stages of the recruitment process".According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions.However, it also found 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments.On top of this, the tech is helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market. 'It's not a level playing field'Image source, EDFImage caption, EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employeesHollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem.EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but decided to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year.Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process."What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't."Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible. It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates.But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews."A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script." One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews. While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would. "I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?"According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says. And while only 16% of employers it surveyed are using AI in the recruitment process, 29% plan to introduce it within the next year. Hollie Moody says EDF does not currently use AI in its recruitment process but may have to in future. For her, the use of AI in job applications remains a "moral dilemma" that employers and candidates will continue to grapple with. But she stresses it cannot replace what her firm is looking for in new recruits."It's about authenticity, but also personality. We want diversity of thought in the business."Get in touchHave you used AI to apply for a job or are you an employer who uses AI to find the best candidate? Share your experiencesCorrection 14 October: This article has been amended to show that according to the ISE's survey 29% of employers plan to introduce AI in the recruitment process over the next year, rather than more than half as we originally reported.

schema.headline: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire

title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
description: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational
body: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational correspondent, Columbus, OhioWarning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicideThe few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood."This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars."You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic WaveExtraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanylImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.Recovery group offering hopeAt the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid."It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood ChurchImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same timeBoth in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose"."In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so."The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope DealersOverdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine."The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.I meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.  "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening."In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters."Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in lettersIn August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moistureOutside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them.In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell.Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs.She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing."Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants.The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous"."Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics."The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it."Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way."'A lot of people are struggling'Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track.It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed."A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail.When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours."She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs."Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics.Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them.Additional reporting by Darren ConwayIf you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis

title: The Diane Watson playground murder: Trauma, loss and a love that endured
description: Pauline tried to help her bleeding friend get home to the flat across the road she shared with her mum, dad and brother Alan.She recalls Diane saying:
body: Pauline tried to help her bleeding friend get home to the flat across the road she shared with her mum, dad and brother Alan.She recalls Diane saying: "I don't believe it. She stabbed me."It was only a short distance to the flat but Pauline felt her friend slumping even before they reached the school gate.With the help of two other girls she got Diane across the road but by the time she reached the entrance to the flat, she collapsed.Her father Jim, who had been alerted by another girl battering on his door, ran down and took his daughter in his arms.He carried her upstairs and desperately tried to revive her as her mother Margaret and 15-year-old brother looked on in horror.Jim tried to give her mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, Pauline said."I'm shouting, 'you're not doing it right'," she said."I could hear her gurgling. There was blood coming out her mouth."The catastrophe inside the Watsons' home sparked a decades' long crusade from Margaret. In the chasm left by her children's deaths, she set out to challenge the power of the media and hold them to account. She said she was not able to rest because of the malicious lies printed about her daughter and demanded an apology from The Herald and Marie Claire. The former dinner lady's campaign brought her into contact with prime ministers, lords, and Hollywood actor Hugh Grant's Hacked Off campaign. It also led to her giving powerful testimony at the Leveson Inquiry into press ethics in November 2011.She told the judge: "Just because a person's died, their reputation shouldn't die with them. "It shouldn't be besmirched at the will of some sick journalist."Pauline says Margaret was small, frail and grieving but she was an "absolute spitfire"."She was a powerhouse but she was driven by grief and anger and rage pretty much the entire time," she said.As we spoke, beside her on the sofa was her husband, Andy Thomson. It took me a moment to take it in when they told me that Andy had been Alan's best friend. That through all the tragedy and trauma, this couple found solace in each other and they've been married for 34 years.Their little grandson is the light of their lives."We were kids and I got what she was going through because I was so close to Alan," says Andy. "And then obviously when Alan passed away, it just drew the two of us even closer. "And we're 34 years together, we're still going strong and always have been. And always will be.""No one gives you a book on how to cope with trauma when you're a teenager," Pauline says. "We were left to cope, and we helped each other. Our life hasn't been all trauma – not at all. But it has been a part of it. "The most important thing for us was we wanted to talk about Diane and Alan, not just the names in the newspapers. "For people to have a better understanding of them as kids – because that's what they were, they were kids. Just normal teenagers who should still be here."If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

schema.headline: The Diane Watson playground murder: Trauma, loss and a love that endured

title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
description: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.Belgium condemned the assault on its consul
body: A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the attack on Levine was "disturbing" and "not a good look".It was also condemned by the US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, who called it a "despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards". A staunch ally of Israel, Huckabee said the assailants must face "prosecution to the fullest extent of the law".In Saturday's incident the European diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice."Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said. "As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. "Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters.""According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground."It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged.""The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

schema.headline: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
